User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Here’s how to handle each item for your 2024 federal return (single filer, Texas), plus which forms you’ll need.

Income and where it goes
- W-2 wages ($68,200): Report from your W-2 on Form 1040.
- Photography income ($16,300): Report on Schedule C (sole proprietorship).
  - You’ll also owe self-employment (SE) tax on your Schedule C profit via Schedule SE. Half of the SE tax becomes an above-the-line deduction on Schedule 1.
- Capital One 360 interest

($2,100): Taxable interest; will be on 1099-INT. Because your total interest/dividends exceed $1,500, you’ll file Schedule B.
- Merrill Edge ($420): If this is interest or dividends, it also goes on Schedule B. If any of it is from selling investments, you’ll also need Form 8949 and Schedule D.

Deductions you can take
- Standard vs itemized: For 2024, the standard deduction for single is $14,600.
  - Your likely itemized deductions appear limited (Texas has no state income tax; you rent; charity is $1,500

; no large medical listed). So the standard deduction should be better than itemizing.
- Student loan interest (Nelnet): You paid $5,100, but the federal above-the-line deduction caps at $2,500 and phases out for 2024 single MAGI between $80,000 and $95,000.
  - Given your numbers, you’ll likely be in that phaseout. Rough estimate of your allowable deduction is about $2,050–$2,200 (depends on your final Schedule C profit and whether the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” are business expenses—see below).
  - Yo

u’ll need Form 1098-E from Nelnet.
- Home office (for the photography business only):
  - You use 120 sq ft exclusively out of 740 sq ft = about 16.2% business use.
  - You pay $1,750/month rent = $21,000/year.
  - Two methods:
    - Actual-expense method (Form 8829): You can deduct the business share of indirect costs. Rent alone would be about $21,000 × 16.2% ≈ $3,406. If you also have utilities, renter’s insurance, and internet, those can be included proportionally too. This generally yields a much large

r deduction than the simplified method for your facts.
    - Simplified method: $5/sq ft × 120 sq ft = $600.
  - The home office deduction can’t create or increase a Schedule C loss; any disallowed amount using the actual method can carry forward.
- “Unreimbursed expenses” ($1,050): Please clarify.
  - If these are photography-business costs (gear, supplies, software, mileage, website, etc.), they are deductible on Schedule C.
  - If they are unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job, they are not ded

uctible federally in 2024 (exceptions: Armed Forces reservist, qualified performing artist, fee-basis government official, impairment-related work expenses).
- Charitable contributions ($1,500 to Salvation Army): Deductible on Schedule A only if you itemize (you likely won’t). Keep the receipt/acknowledgment.

Other items that likely help you
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: You should qualify for up to 20% of your qualified business income (from the photography Schedule C), claimed on Form 8995

. Roughly, if your Schedule C profit is around $11,800 after expenses, the QBI deduction could be around $2,200 (final amount depends on your exact profit and other adjustments).
- Half of SE tax: Deductible above-the-line on Schedule 1 automatically when you complete Schedule SE.

Forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (additional income/adjustments: includes student loan interest deduction and half SE tax; Schedule C also flows through here)
- Schedule C (photography business)
- Schedule SE (se

lf-employment tax)
- Schedule 2 (carries your SE tax to Form 1040)
- Schedule B (interest/dividends, since total > $1,500)
- Form 8829 (home office actual-expense method) or use the simplified method (no separate form)
- Form 8995 (QBI deduction)
- Schedule A only if you itemize (unlikely here)
- If you sold investments: Form 8949 and Schedule D

Quick estimates to guide decisions
- Standard deduction vs itemizing: Standard ($14,600) will almost certainly beat itemizing for you.
- Home office method: Actual

-expense method appears better than the simplified one given your rent; just remember it’s limited by your business profit.
- Student loan interest: Expect a partial deduction (approx $2,050–$2,200), subject to the $2,500 cap and phaseout.

Open questions so I can tighten the numbers
- Is the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” for your photography business or your W-2 job?
- The $420 from Merrill Edge: was it interest, dividends, or did you sell any investments?
- Do you have other home office indirect costs (u

tilities, renter’s insurance, internet) or direct office costs (e.g., a desk used only in the office) we should include?
- Did you buy any photography gear or software in 2024 (which could be expensed or depreciated on Schedule C)?

Note: This is general guidance based on 2024 federal rules. If you’d like, I can run a tighter estimate once you confirm the open items above.
